turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning. I'll just get your blood pressure before Dr Shah comes in, if you pop your arm out.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, go on. Whole thing's a fuss, if you ask me.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Reading is one hundred and fifty-eight over ninety-four. Pulse seventy-six. Oxygen sats ninety-eight percent. Temperature thirty-six point six.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): See? Not exactly an emergency.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): He'll be through in a minute. I'll leave the door.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry we're late, the car park was rammed. I'm his wife. And don't let him shrug the cough off, it's been dreadful at night.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): It's a tickle. Leftover from a cold. Hardly worth the chair.
[SEG0008] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Shah. Have a seat. What would you like to start with?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Surgery rang about my high blood pressure tablet. I've had it for years. And she dragged me in over this cough, which is nothing.
[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Alright. The cough, in your own words, what's it like?
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Dry. No gunk. Tickly, mostly when I'm in bed. I had a cold, so that's all it is.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been—
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks. If that. I'm not sitting here counting days.
[SEG0014] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two weeks my foot. It's six weeks easy, since before the bank holiday. I hear it every night.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): So you're saying about a fortnight, and you're saying six weeks. Dry, and worse in bed. Any phlegm with it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Bone dry. Nothing to cough up.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any breathlessness? Getting puffed out?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm fine. I walk the dog every morning, no bother.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): And chest pain, or any wheeze?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. No wheezing. Tail of a cold, like I said.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He stops halfway up the hill by Tesco now. He never used to.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): That's just being sixty-two and lazy. Well, actually, the stairs at home, I do get a bit puffed. It passes. Not worth mentioning.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): So a bit short of breath on the stairs, no chest pain, no wheeze. Any fever, feeling hot or shivery?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I haven't felt hot. No shivers.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): The cold itself, sore throat, runny nose, has that cleared?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, gone. Nose was a couple of days, that's it. Cough just sat there after.
[SEG0027] person_4 (DOCTOR): When did the new blood pressure tablet start?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Um. Recent. After the last check. I can't put a date on it. Sometime lately.
[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I thought it was after his birthday, but I wasn't in the room, so don't ask me the day.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the date open. What's the tablet called?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril, for my blood pressure. Not the one my brother has. He's on lisinopril for his blood pressure, swears by it, but that's his.
[SEG0032] person_4 (DOCTOR): What dose are you on?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Five milligrams of ramipril, or ten. I think they said five, maybe, taken in the morning.
[SEG0034] person_4 (DOCTOR): Every day?
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He leaves it on the counter and then—
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Most mornings, yeah. If I'm out early with the dog I forget the odd one. Couldn't swear I'm doing it right.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): Anything else you're taking?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): A statin. Little white tablet. Don't ask me the name, atorva-something, no, I'm guessing, scrub that.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And before the ramipril he was on amlodipine for the blood pressure. They stopped it, his ankles blew up.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Ages ago. Not on that now. Ankles are fine.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any allergy to medicines?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing I know of.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Didn't you get a rash with penicillin as a kid? Your mum always said.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): That was donkey's years ago and I'm not even sure it was the penicillin. I've had amoxicillin since, no problem. So no allergies.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll note no known drug allergy, and that the penicillin story isn't agreed. Let me have a listen to your chest. Deep breaths.
[SEG0046] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear, no crackles, no wheeze. Heart sounds are normal. Ankles aren't swollen today.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): Told you. Fit as anything.

[SEG0048] person_4 (DOCTOR): Blood pressure today is still up, one hundred and fifty-eight over ninety-four, on what may be five milligrams of ramipril. My first thought is we increase the ramipril to ten milligrams, and I'll book a chest x-ray for the cough.
[SEG0049] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The cough only really got going after he started that tablet, though. Before that it was just the sniffles.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, yeah, maybe. I didn't clock it. Still think it's the cold.
[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): That changes things. I'm not going to increase an ACE inhibitor if the cough may be from it. Scratch the higher dose, and we'll hold the x-ray for now.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): So I just carry on, then? It's not even that bad.
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): No. I'd like you to stop the ramipril from today. We'll switch you to losartan for the blood pressure, fifty milligrams, once a day, by mouth.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Losartan. Right. Another tablet to forget.
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'm not pinning a diagnosis on the cough. It might be the ramipril, it might just be the tail of that cold. I can't say which.
[SEG0056] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And if it doesn't stop?

[SEG0057] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in four weeks either way, and we'll see whether the cough has eased after the switch. If you're gasping at rest, or you get chest pain, don't wait, get help the same day.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah. It won't come to that.
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll also arrange a kidney blood test, urea and electrolytes, before we get too far with the losartan. The nurse can sort the form.
[SEG0060] person_1 (NURSE): I can print that at the desk on your way out.
[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): Smoking. Where are we with that?
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Packed it in. Five-ish years ago. Don't miss it.
[SEG0063] person_4 (DOCTOR): And alcohol?
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Odd pint at the weekend. Nothing silly. She's worse than me with the wine, mind.
[SEG0065] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Cheek. One glass.

[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Dry cough, you're calling it about two weeks, your wife says six, worse at night, no phlegm, a bit puffed on the stairs, no pain, no wheeze, no fever. Ramipril, possibly five milligrams, timing unclear, odd doses missed. We're stopping it, starting losartan fifty milligrams daily, bloods for the kidneys, and I'll see you in four weeks, with no firm label on the cough.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): If you say so. Still reckon it's the cold.
[SEG0068] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll make sure he actually picks the new one up from the chemist.
[SEG0069] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. Prescription will go to the chemist this afternoon. Off you go.

spec.situation: Hypertension patient with a dry cough for weeks that they connect to 'a cold'; recently started ramipril or enalapril; they mention a relative's lisinopril. Doctor thinks aloud, changes the drug but does not give a firm diagnosis of the cough.
features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

bad.reason: Sore throat was asked about, but patient did not mention having had it.

omissions.text: Breathlessness was specifically denied at first for walking the dog/no bother, before the patient later acknowledged mild breathlessness on the stairs.
The planned chest X-ray was initially proposed for the cough, then explicitly cancelled/held for now after concern that the cough may be due to ramipril.
The wife reported the cough only really got going after he started ramipril; this timing concern changed management.
The patient reported having had amoxicillin since the childhood penicillin story, with no problem.
Ramipril was not just uncertain between 5 mg and 10 mg; the doctor's assessment noted he was on what may be 5 mg of ramipril when discussing management.

omissions.text: The cough is specifically worse at night as reported by the wife ('dreadful at night') and summarised by the doctor, not just mostly when in bed.
The doctor initially proposed increasing ramipril to 10 mg because blood pressure remained high on the current dose before changing plan due to possible ACE-inhibitor cough.
